summary.title: Efficient and Flexible Integration of Variant Characteristics in Rare Variant Association Studies Using Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation
summary.authors: Hana Susak, Laura Serra-Saurina, Raquel Rabionet Janssen, Laura Domènech, Mattia Bosio, Francesc Muyas, Xavier Estivill, Georgia Escaramís, Stephan Ossowski
summary.type_of_paper: Methods/software with benchmarking and application study
summary.executive_summary: Rare variants (RVs) are hypothesized to contribute substantially to the heritability of complex diseases, yet rare variant association studies (RVAS) frequently lack statistical power, particularly in small-to-medium cohorts and when variants explain only a small fraction of phenotypic variance. Existing RVAS tests include burden tests, variance-component tests (SKAT, C-alpha), linear-combination tests (SKAT-O), and Bayesian approaches such as the hierarchical Bayesian multiple regression model (HBMR) and the mixed-effects test (MiST). A central limitation of MiST is that full-model inference requires multiple integration, making it computationally intractable for genome-wide scans, so a score test is used instead. This paper introduces BATI, a Bayesian rare variant association test based on Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation (INLA), implemented within the rvGWAS framework. Unlike prior methods, BATI flexibly incorporates individual or variant-specific features (categorical and numeric covariates) while performing inference based on full model estimation, and it is substantially faster and more accurate than MCMC. The authors developed a 'semi-synthetic' whole-exome sequencing (WES) cohort simulator that combines thousands of real WES datasets with ClinVar-derived disease risk variants, enabling realistic benchmarking. They report that BATI outperforms established RVAS methods, achieving power above 75% in scenarios where competing tests fail, such as when risk variants in sum explain less than 0.5% of phenotypic variance. Applying rvGWAS to a Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL) study, they identified eight candidate predisposition genes, including EHMT2 and COPS7A. The paper proposes using the difference in deviance information criterion (ΔDIC) for model selection, with a suggested threshold of ΔDIC > 10, calibrated via simulations using S = 10 randomly shuffled datasets. judge_context:
Executive Summary
Rare variants (RVs) are hypothesized to contribute substantially to the heritability of complex diseases, yet rare variant association studies (RVAS) frequently lack statistical power, particularly in small-to-medium cohorts and when variants explain only a small fraction of phenotypic variance. Existing RVAS tests include burden tests, variance-component tests (SKAT, C-alpha), linear-combination tests (SKAT-O), and Bayesian approaches such as the hierarchical Bayesian multiple regression model (HBMR) and the mixed-effects test (MiST). A central limitation of MiST is that full-model inference requires multiple integration, making it computationally intractable for genome-wide scans, so a score test is used instead. This paper introduces BATI, a Bayesian rare variant association test based on Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation (INLA), implemented within the rvGWAS framework. Unlike prior methods, BATI flexibly incorporates individual or variant-specific features (categorical and numeric covariates) while performing inference based on full model estimation, and it is substantially faster and more accurate than MCMC. The authors developed a 'semi-synthetic' whole-exome sequencing (WES) cohort simulator that combines thousands of real WES datasets with ClinVar-derived disease risk variants, enabling realistic benchmarking. They report that BATI outperforms established RVAS methods, achieving power above 75% in scenarios where competing tests fail, such as when risk variants in sum explain less than 0.5% of phenotypic variance. Applying rvGWAS to a Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL) study, they identified eight candidate predisposition genes, including EHMT2 and COPS7A. The paper proposes using the difference in deviance information criterion (ΔDIC) for model selection, with a suggested threshold of ΔDIC > 10, calibrated via simulations using S = 10 randomly shuffled datasets. This summary reflects the provided text; the bibliography is absent, so top_influential_citations is set to an empty string.

Research Context
Rare variants are implicated in complex disease etiology and missing heritability. RVAS aggregate rare variants within functional units to gain power. Burden tests assume one-sided effects, which is often violated. Variance-component tests handle heterogeneous effects but were later combined into SKAT-O. Bayesian methods like MiST use variant characteristics but are computationally heavy. INLA offers a faster, more accurate alternative to MCMC for Bayesian inference. Prior benchmarks relied on artificial simulations lacking realistic noise.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether BATI improves RVAS power while remaining computationally feasible. BATI should flexibly integrate variant characteristics as covariates. BATI should perform inference based on full model estimation. BATI should outperform existing RVAS methods, especially with functional annotation. BATI should cope with complex population structure and confounders. ΔDIC should enable robust model selection between null and alternative models. BATI should achieve high power even when variants explain little variance. The predicted outcome is that BATI identifies risk genes missed by other tests.

Methodological Details
The study is based at The Barcelona Institute of Science and Technology. The framework is rvGWAS, supporting WES or WGS data. rvGWAS integrates QC, filtering, stratification detection, and functional annotations. rvGWAS includes four existing tests plus two Bayesian alternatives. A new semi-synthetic WES cohort simulator was developed. The simulator combines thousands of real WES datasets with ClinVar risk variants. Two large datasets formed the basis of the simulation. 1000GP samples were split half as cases and half as controls. The Iberian cohort used one third cases and two thirds controls. Breast cancer risk variants were queried from ClinVar. Variants with MAF higher than 0.01 were removed. Exome databases EVS, 1000GP, and ExAC were used for filtering.

Procedures And Architectures
BATI uses INLA for Bayesian inference on latent Gaussian models. INLA was implemented via the R package INLA version 17.06.20. BATI integrates categorical and numeric variant characteristics as covariates. The null hypothesis assumes no genetic effects. The alternative hypothesis includes variant-specific effects. Model goodness of fit is assessed via the Deviance Information Criteria. ΔDIC is used as the model selection criterion. A ΔDIC threshold greater than 10 is recommended. Significance thresholds were derived from 10 random cohort splits. Thresholds correspond to TIER levels of 5%, 0.1%, and 0.01%. S = 10 datasets were used for robust threshold estimation. Power analyses were run across 100 simulations per gene.

Key Results
BATI outperforms existing methods on realistic semi-synthetic cohorts. BATI achieves power above 75% where competing tests fail. High power is maintained when variants explain less than 0.5% variance. BATI power exceeds 75% in low-variance-explained scenarios. BATI power is stable despite smaller cohort size. At 0.5% VE and 0.01% TIER, BATI reaches near-100% power. Median power for three risk genes at 0.5% VE is 55%. BATI identifies most genes at 0.5% VE with TIER 0.01%. BATI identifies all genes at TIER 0.1% with greater than 80% power. Burden, KBAC, and SKAT-O fail to call BRCA2. HBMR fails to call BARD1, CHEK2, and PALB2 at TIER 0.1%. MiST fails to identify any risk gene at low VE or low TIER.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
BATI benefits strongly from incorporating variant characteristics. BATI strongly benefits from including covariates. BATI gains power when risk genes contain mostly loss-of-function variants. BATI performs at least as well as other methods for missense variants. Semi-synthetic cohorts better reflect realistic noise than pure simulations. ΔDIC enables robust model selection between null and alternative models. BATI represents a flexible testing approach extensible in the future.

Contradictions And Limitations
BATI's advantage depends on incorporating meaningful biological context. Some methods perform worse due to smaller cohort size. Power differences are more pronounced at low variance-explained levels. MiST's poor performance may stem from zero-inflated p-values. The benchmark relies on semi-synthetic data, which may not fully represent real-world complexity. The ΔDIC threshold of 10 is a rule of thumb requiring simulation calibration.

Claims
BATI outperforms existing RVAS methods on realistic semi-synthetic cohorts, especially with functional annotation. BATI outperforms established RVAS methods on realistic, semi-synthetic whole-exome sequencing cohorts. BATI substantially outperforms existing methods if prior information on the effect of variants on protein function is used. BATI achieves power above 75% in scenarios in which competing tests fail. Most tests perform slightly worse due to the smaller size of the cohort. BATI's advantage depends on incorporating meaningful biological context. BATI represents a flexible testing approach that can be further extended and enhanced in the future. It enables identification of candidate predisposition genes in real studies.
BATI is computationally efficient and accurate compared to MCMC-based Bayesian inference. INLA is a non-sampling based numerical approximation procedure. INLA is also more accurate than MCMC when given the same computational resources. INLA renders INLA substantially faster than MCMC. Evaluating the convergence of MCMC sampling chains is not straightforward. BATI enables full model estimation for genome-wide scans. It avoids the computational intractability of full-model inference in MiST.
Semi-synthetic cohorts provide more realistic benchmarks than pure simulations. Simulated variant data is well-known to lack the complexity and noise-level of real data. We combined real WES cohorts, representing realistic background noise, with real disease variants. Pure simulations result in overly optimistic benchmark performances. The benchmark relies on semi-synthetic data, which may not fully represent real-world complexity. It enables testing of different disease architectures with various variance-explained levels. It facilitates translation of method-specific significance thresholds to comparable thresholds.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
BATI's performance is stable despite the smaller cohort size.

Ethical Considerations
The study uses ClinVar-derived risk variants for simulation. The study uses real WES datasets from various studies.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 3 shows gene-wise power plots for the 1000GP cohort. Table 2 reports power across genes and TIER thresholds. Supplementary S6 Fig shows estimated thresholds across 10 splits. Supplementary S8 Fig shows results for the Iberian cohort. Supplementary S9 Fig shows gene-wise power for the Iberian cohort.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is BATI, a Bayesian RVAS test using INLA that flexibly integrates variant characteristics. 2. The strongest evidence is BATI achieving power above 75% where competing tests fail. 3. The future path is extending BATI as a flexible testing approach.
